vignette:
She works the afternoon shift at a busy Thai restaurant downtown. The lunch rush has ended, and the dining room is quiet except for the clatter of dishes from the kitchen. She moves between tables, refilling water glasses and clearing plates, but her eyes keep drifting toward the front window. Every time a car slows down outside, her shoulders tighten. She knows he does not come here anymore-he never did, not to the restaurant itself-but the feeling of being watched has never left her.

Two years ago, she was still married, living in a small apartment near the train station. She had just started a new waitressing job at a different place, a no-frills noodle house where she worked the evening shift. He was a customer at first, a middle-aged man who came in alone every Tuesday and Thursday, always ordering the same dish. He smiled a lot, asked her name, left generous tips. She did not think much of it at first. Other customers were friendly too.

Then he started coming on other days. He would sit at the same table, watch her as she worked. One night, as she left through the back door after closing, she saw him standing under the streetlight across the alley, staring. She felt a cold wash of fear but told herself she was imagining things. She quickened her pace and did not look back.

After that, he began appearing outside her apartment. Not every night, but often enough that she started checking the street before unlocking the door. He left notes under her windshield wiper: "You look so beautiful when you work." "I miss you when you're not there." She threw them away, but the handwriting stayed burned into her mind. Her husband at the time told her she was overreacting, that it was just a lonely man with no boundaries. She stopped talking about it.

The stalking escalated. He called the restaurant, asked for her by name, hung up when someone else answered. He sent flowers with no card. Once, she found a photograph of herself standing at the bus stop, taken from a distance, slipped under her welcome mat. That was the night she called the police. They took a report, but nothing changed. No arrest, no warning. Just a file number on a piece of paper she still keeps in a drawer.

She divorced her husband a few months later-not because of the stalking, though the strain certainly did not help. The marriage had been failing for years. She moved to a new apartment across town, changed jobs to the current restaurant, and blocked every unknown number on her phone. She thought that would be the end.

But her body does not seem to know it is over. At work, she startles at the sound of a dropped spoon. She finds herself scanning every customer's face as they walk through the door, cataloging details-build, hair color, jacket style-then forcing herself to stop. Sometimes a man with a similar build will sit alone, and her heart pounds so hard she has to retreat to the kitchen and take deep breaths until the fear passes. Her manager has noticed that she flinches when a customer touches her arm to get her attention. She has not told anyone why.

Her sleep is broken. She wakes most nights around 3:00 a.m., certain she heard a footstep or a creak in the hallway. She lies still, barely breathing, listening until the silence feels almost worse than a noise would. Some nights she checks the locks three times before she can close her eyes again. She does not date, does not answer social media messages from people she does not know, and has changed her schedule to avoid the evening shifts that remind her of the noodle house.

The worst part, she told her therapist last week, is the constant feeling of being hunted. Even now, as she wipes down a table and glances out the window, there is no one there. But her chest is tight, and she is already planning how she will leave-through the front, into the bright sun, past the cars that might have someone sitting inside. She waits until another waiter offers to walk her out. She always says yes.
